linkedin.title: The biggest problem with news today is not that we have too little of it, but that we have too much.
linkedin.body:
We are drowning in information. Most news apps try to solve this by showing you more of what you already like. They create echo chambers that confirm your biases rather than challenging your perspective. That is not personalization. That is just curation.

At Headlinne, we think the future of news is about context, not just content. It is about understanding the 'why' behind a story and how it connects to the bigger picture. We are building a roadmap that prioritizes clarity over speed. Our goal is to help you understand complex topics without having to spend hours digging through multiple sources.

Personalization should mean getting smarter, not just getting more comfortable. It means finding the right balance between what you need to know and what you want to know. We are moving away from algorithms that simply chase engagement and toward tools that respect your time and intelligence.

We are iterating on this every day. It is a slow process to get right, but it is the only way to build something that actually adds value.
linkedin.cta: You can see where we are heading and try the app for yourself at HEADLINNE.com.

story_card.headline: Lab-grown brain cells show signs of aging
story_card.standfirst: Scientists have kept human brain cells alive for seven years to study how they age.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text: Scientists grew tiny clumps of human brain cells that successfully aged over seven years.

steps.label: How we got here
steps.text: Researchers maintained these peppercorn-sized samples in a lab setting for a record duration.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.text: The cells appeared to track the passage of time just like brains inside a living human head.

steps.label: What to watch
steps.text: Future research will determine if this method can unlock new secrets about brain aging.

story_card.caption:
Scientists have successfully grown human brain cells in a lab that age just like a real brain.

These tiny samples were kept alive for seven years, setting a new record. By observing how they change over time, researchers hope to better understand the natural aging process of the human mind.

Would you want to know exactly how your brain is aging, or would you prefer not to know?
